limitations_and_boundaries: GEARS's ability to predict outcomes for perturbing previously unperturbed genes is limited if those genes are not well connected in the knowledge graph.
GEARS uses a Bayesian formulation to output an uncertainty metric inversely correlated with model performance.

research_questions.statement: Can a deep learning method integrating a gene–gene knowledge graph predict transcriptional responses to single and multigene perturbations, including unseen combinations?

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS significantly outperformed all baselines on both datasets with an m.s.e. improvement of 30–50%

claims.statement: GEARS outperforms baselines in predicting single-gene perturbation transcriptional responses.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS improved precision@10 by more than 40% for four of five genetic interaction subtypes, and the improvement exceeded 90% for redundancy and epistasis

claims.statement: GEARS predicts non-additive combinatorial perturbation effects better than existing methods.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS improves performance by more than 30% across all cases, with the highest improvement of 53% observed when both perturbed genes in the combination are unseen.

claims.statement: GEARS predicts multigene perturbation outcomes even when genes are unseen during training.

experiments_or_tasks: Compare GEARS against baselines: no perturbation, gene regulatory network (CellOracle), and CPA.
Compare GEARS against baselines using precision@10 and top ten accuracy.
Define five genetic interaction subtypes: synergy, suppression, neomorphism, redundancy, epistasis.
Define three generalization classes: zero unseen, one unseen, two unseen genes in combination.
Evaluate GEARS on held-out single-gene perturbations from Perturb-seq screens in RPE-1 and K562 cells.
Evaluate GEARS on predicting genetic interaction scores and top-ranked interactions.
Evaluate GEARS on two-gene perturbations from Norman et al. Perturb-seq dataset (131 two-gene perturbations).
